$comment: ★★ DSS's OWN COMMON BESIDE A WEAK DEFINITION OF ITS NAME ON ELF: THE COMMON STANDS (P69 fold 3b; D-C-TENTATIVE-DEFINITIONS-OF-ONE-NAME-IN-TWO-UNITS-REFUSED) -- `examples/c/common_beside_a_weak_definition_elf` with the COMMON written by DSS: main.c's `int dss_tentative;` is a tentative definition, which a unit compiled for a document that states commons writes as a COMMON, as gcc does under `-fcommon`. The one object named to the link is gcc's build of `__attribute__((weak)) int dss_tentative = 5;` (`OBJECT WEAK`, in `.data`). The ELF documents' `commonYieldsTo: strongDefinition` keeps the common over a weak definition, and the program reads 0, exit 37 -- the answer GNU ld gives gcc's own common beside the same object (✔MEASURED 2026-10-08, both orders, x86_64 natively and aarch64 under qemu-aarch64). This example pins the RANK of a common DSS writes, not the form: a zero-filled strong definition (what the unit wrote before P69 fold 3b) also outranks a weak one and also reads 0; the cells that tell the two forms apart on ELF -- two DSS objects of one name, and a DSS object beside gcc's own `int v;` or `int v = 7;` under GNU ld -- are `link/test_tentative_definitions_as_commons`'s. The `release` arm pins that optimizing the unit changes nothing about which of the two the program reads.
